before.text: In towns across Europe, stone memorials list local soldiers who died in the war of 1914 to 1918.
That war began with one shooting, on 28 June 1914.
Within about five weeks, five of Europe's great powers were at war.
So how did one shooting start a world war?
Picture a scuffle on a crowded street, where both fighters have friends who promised to back them up.
One shove, and the friends pile in, then their friends too.
In 1914, the shove was the assassination, and the two fighters were Austria-Hungary and Serbia.
The friends were their allies and protectors.
Here are the countries, left to right, in the order they went to war.
The armbands show the alliance system: Germany was Austria-Hungary's ally, and Russia was France's.
Those promises meant a war between two powers could drag in their partners.
First, the background.
For years, the great powers practiced militarism, building huge armies and detailed war plans.
Britain and Germany even raced to build giant battleships called dreadnoughts.
So by 1914, every great power was armed and could mobilize fast.
Next comes the spark, in Sarajevo.
Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary's throne, rode through the city in an open car.
Gavrilo Princip, a nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb, shot and killed him.
Princip was driven by nationalism: he wanted South Slavs living under Austria-Hungary united with Serbia.
Back on the line, Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia.
With Germany's promise of full support, it declared war on Serbia on 28 July.
But Russia saw itself as Serbia's protector, so it began mobilization, calling up its huge army.
What do you think Germany, Austria-Hungary's ally, did next?
On 1 August, it declared war on Russia, then on Russia's ally France two days later.
A common mistake is to think the assassination alone caused the war.
It was only the spark: the alliance system and militarism turned one quarrel into a war among great powers.
Now, why did Britain join in?
Germany's Schlieffen Plan aimed to beat France quickly, to avoid fighting on two fronts at once.
Its army would sweep through Belgium, a neutral country.
But in 1839, Britain had promised to protect Belgium's neutrality.
So when German troops entered Belgium on 4 August, Britain declared war on Germany that same day.
A single assassination became a world war because alliances and war plans pulled each great power in, one after another.
One shooting started a war between Austria-Hungary and Serbia, and promises of backup pulled in Russia, Germany, France and Britain.
